div.p: Background. Desmoplastic infantile ganglioglioma/astrocytoma (DIG/DIA) is a rare, low-grade tumor of infants. They are usually composed of a mixed astrocytic and neuronal component with desmoplastic stroma and embryonal-looking areas. Despite some recent reports, clinical, morphological and molecular features of DIG/DIAs are still not well characterized. Here, we present a series of 8 DIG/DIA cases. Methods. Hacettepe University and Koc University Hospital, Departments of Pathology, databases were screened for DIG/DIA. Eight patients were identified. All the slides were reevaluated, and patients' clinical data were obtained. All cases were tested for BRAF V600 mutation and 3 BRAF V600 wild-type cases were sequenced. Results. Median age at the diagnosis was 5.5 months (4-30 months). The female to male ratio was 6:2. Two cases recurred. Four cases showed BRAF p. V600 mutation. Of those BRAF p. V600 wild-type cases, one harbored TMEM-106B::BRAF fusion, described for the first time in a DIG/DIA case. Conclusions. DIG/DIA is a low-grade tumor seen in early childhood and characterized by an indolent clinical course. The most common molecular signature of these tumors is BRAF alterations, including rearrangements. The primary differential diagnosis is infant-type hemispheric glioma and given the similarities, pathologists must remain careful to ensure accurate diagnosis.

Central nervous system (CNS) tumors are the second most common neoplasms in children after leukemias, and gliomas comprise the majority of CNS tumors in children. 1 The classification of CNS tumors has changed substantially over time and 2021 WHO classification has grouped glial and glioneuronal/neuronal tumors into 5 major categories: adult-type diffuse gliomas, pediatric-type diffuse gliomas, circumscribed astrocytic gliomas, glioneuronal/neuronal tumors, and ependymal tumors. 2 In daily neuropathology practice, circumscribed astrocytic tumors, especially pilocytic astrocytoma, are the most frequently encountered tumors in children. 3 Desmoplastic infantile gangliogliomas/astrocytomas (DIG/DIA), by contrast, are one of the rarest tumor types and occur almost exclusively in infants. 4 DIG/DIA was first described in the 1980s as an infantile tumor with characteristic features reported as mesenchymal appearance and frequent meningothelial involvement. 5 Later studies elaborated its features in much detail such as its biphasic morphology and its molecular background. 4,[6][7][8] These tumors are driven by mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK) pathway alterations, most commonly SNVs or insertions/deletions (InDels) in the BRAF (B-Rapidly Accelerated Fibrosarcoma) gene 9,10 and as recently described, some cases with RAF1/BRAF fusions. 11,12 Morphologically these tumors have a biphasic morphology; desmoplastic areas with rich reticulin network in-between spindly cells and areas of tumor with an almost embryonal appearance with high cellularity and variable amount of mitosis. DIG/DIAs present as large hemispheric masses with increasing head circumference. Because it is rare, only small series with limited number of cases have been published. Moreover, differential diagnosis of these tumors has become extremely important after the characterization of other infantile tumors, especially those with receptor tyrosine kinase gene fusions. 13,14 Here, we report a series of 8 cases of DIG/DIA with their morphological, immunohistochemical, molecular, and clinical features.

div.head: Methods
div.p: The pathology databases of Hacettepe University Hospital and Koç University Hospital were screened for DIG/DIA cases between 2000 and 2024. A total of 8 patients were identified. All the slides were reevaluated by 3 neuropathologists (I.K., B.B., and F.S.), and patients' demographic and follow-up data (until February 2025) were obtained from hospitals' electronic patient databases. Morphological features (growth pattern, percentage of primitive areas and desmoplastic areas, presence of neuronal/ganglionic component, number of mitoses, presence of subpial dissemination) were noted.

div.head: Immunohistochemistry
div.p: Immunohistochemistry studies using antibodies against glial fibrillary acid protein (GFAP), oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2 (OLIG2 ), neurofilament protein, synaptophysin, Chromogranin A, Ki67, anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), ROS1, pan-TRK were performed. Details of the select antibodies and platforms used are listed in Table 1.

div.head: Molecular Studies
div.p: A real-time PCR-based BRAF V600 mutation analysis was performed in all cases using AmoyDx BRAF Mutation Analysis Kit V2 (Amoy Diagnostics Co., Ltd, China). This kit is specifically manufactured to detect BRAF V600 alterations in DNA samples isolated from FFPE tissue. Seven different mutations can be detected by this kit (p.V600E c.1799T>A, c.1799_1800TG>AA; p.V600K, c.1798_1799GT>AA; p.V600R c.1798_1799GT>AG; p.V600D, c.1799_1800TG>AC, c.1799_1800TG>AT; p.V600A c.1799T>C). For the mutation-specific real-time PCR study, 5 × 6 µm thick sections were obtained from paraffin blocks that have at least 20% tumor cell content. DNA was isolated using QIAamp DNA FFPE Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). Samples were measured and checked for the purity by Nanodrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). PCR was performed according to the manufacturer's instructions, and positivity thresholds were applied as specified in the manual.

div.head: Importance of the study
div.p: Desmoplastic infantile ganglioglioma/astrocytoma (DIG/ DIA) is a rare pediatric tumor with limited information in the literature. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of 8 cases with long clinical follow up and these tumors' molecular landscape. TMEM106B::BRAF fusion is shown for the first time in DIG/DIA. Although high-grade looking primitive morphology is commonly observed in DIG/ DIA cases, our series did not show any associated adverse clinical outcome. Our study emphasizes the importance of molecular testing, specifically RNA-based fusion panels, as BRAF fusions can be observed in cases without BRAF single-nucleotide variant (SNV). These insights reinforce the need for broader molecular characterization of DIG/ DIA and will aid pathologists and clinicians in distinguishing it from other infantile gliomas, supporting more accurate diagnosis and treatment planning.

div.head: Kulac et al.: Morphomolecular and clinical evaluation of DIG/DIAs
Next-Generation Sequencing Studies
div.p: Because the major differential diagnosis of DIG/DIA is infant-type hemispheric glioma (IHG), next-generation sequencing was performed using Illumina TruSight RNA Pan-Cancer Panel (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) to evaluate receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) fusions, a signature finding of IHG. This hybrid-capture panel is designed to detect known and novel fusions and includes all exons of 1385 genes, and has been used for fusion detection in brain tumors by other researchers. 15,16 For this study 5 × 6 µm thick sections were obtained from paraffin blocks that have at least 20% tumor cell content. RNA was isolated using Qiagen AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). RNA samples were measured by Qubit Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Libraries were constructed following manufacturer's protocol, and the sequencing was performed on NovaSeq 6000. Data were retrieved and analyzed in BaseSpace Sequencing Hub (Illumina, San Diego, California, United States). Raw sequencing data were analyzed by DRAGEN RNA (v4.3), DRAGEN RNA Pipeline (v3.7), and RNA-Seq Alignment (v.2) of Illumina DRAGEN v3. After demultiplexing, data were mapped and aligned to GRCh37 and fusions were called with the pipelines mentioned. The minimum number of reads required was 10 million per sample with a mapping rate of >90%.

A confirmation study was also conducted for all BRAF V600 wild-type cases to increase the accuracy of the findings. In this study, RNA isolated for the TruSight RNA Pan-Cancer study was used and complementary cDNAs synthesized. Later, libraries were constructed using the ArcherDx FusionPlex Lung V2 panel (ArcherDx, Boulder, CO, US) following manufacturers protocol. This panel is an amplicon based hot spot targeted panel and is designed to detect known and novel fusions in involving specific genes including BRAF, MET, ROS1, ALK, NTRK1/2/3; that has been used in many studies in the literature. 17 ,18 The workflow for molecular analysis is outlined in Figure 1.

div.head: Basic Demographics and Clinical Features of the Cases
div.p: A total of 8 cases were included. All but one were infants at initial diagnosis and median age at diagnosis was 5.5 months (4-30 months). The exception was a female diagnosed at 30 months old. Male to female ratio was 6:2. Median follow-up was 68 months (10-95 months); although one case lost follow-up after the surgery. Two cases (cases #4 and #6) recurred in 11 and 3 months after the initial surgery, respectively. Radiologically all tumors were located in the hemispheres, parietal and temporal lobes being the most common regions (2 cases at each region), and in the 4 remaining cases tumors were located in frontal, frontoparietal, temporoparietal, and frontotemporal regions. All cases but 2 underwent gross total resection. Those 2 with near-total resection are being followed with stable residues. One of the cases that recurred received chemotherapy (temozolomide) after the second surgery and has no evidence of any recurrent tumor at last follow-up. Demographic and clinical features of cases are listed in Table 2 in details.

div.head: Histomorphological Characteristics
div.p: All cases exhibited the classical biphasic morphology with neuroepithelial cellular component and a dense collagen-rich desmoplastic stroma. Neuroepithelial component was composed of spindly astrocytic cells that display fascicular and/ or storiform patterns. Neuroepithelial component in all cases harbored neuronal component that is highlighted by positive synaptophysin staining and also in some cases rare ganglionic differentiation was observed on H&E sections. However, in all cases, a notable presence of primitive, embryonal-like morphology was evident. This primitive component, lacking desmoplasia, is composed of small cells with relatively scant cytoplasm.

div.head: Extent and features of primitive-looking areas
div.p: All cases had both desmoplastic and primitive areas but the proportion of each varied (Figure 2). The evidently primitive-looking areas were less prevalent, comprising not more than 50% (most being 10%-20%) of the total tumor area in all cases. We also examined the mitotic count in each tumor, only in the primitive areas, which ranged from 3 to 40 (median: 12.5) per 10 high power fields (HPF) or mm 2 (mitotic count was evaluated using an Olympus BX53 microscope, 10 HPF virtually equals to 1 mm 2 ). The case with the highest mitotic count also had the most pronounced primitive-looking area (case #5).

div.head: Growth pattern
div.p: While these tumors are commonly known to be well-circumscribed only with leptomeningeal involvement, our series reveals subtle variations from this conventional view. Some exhibited widely infiltrative borders, while others presented only focal infiltration of the neighboring neural parenchyma (Figure 3). Drawing parallels with other low-grade, well-circumscribed glial tumors-such as pilocytic astrocytoma-it becomes evident that the assumption of strict circumscription requires reconsideration. This is crucial, especially in distinguishing cases resembling infant-type hemispheric glioma-a tumor type categorized under diffuse pediatric high-grade gliomas-when molecular testing is not accessible. Essentially, the presence of infiltrative borders does not rule out DIG/DIA.

In addition to above-mentioned basic morphological features, 3 of our 8 tumors had subpial/leptomeningeal dissemination. One case had accompanying disorganization of cortical lamination in the neighboring cortex. One case had malformed subpial vasculature.

div.head: Immunohistochemistry
div.p: In all cases, astrocytic areas exhibited staining for GFAP and OLIG2. Additionally, the neuronal as well as ganglionic component was evident through the positive staining for synaptophysin and chromogranin. Primitive areas were negative for GFAP, OLIG2, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. Furthermore, silver impregnation prominently highlighted the reticulin-rich background of desmoplastic areas in all cases. The Ki67 proliferation index correlated with the mitotic count, with the highest Ki67 index reaching 15% in 2 cases.

div.head: Results of mutation specific real-time PCR studies
div.p: Four cases harbored BRAF p. V600E (cases #1, #2, #4, #8) whereas the remaining 4 were negative for BRAF p. V600 on real-time PCR.

div.head: Results of NGS studies
div.p: A comprehensive targeted RNA sequencing analysis was planned to be performed on four cases that tested negative by real-time PCR (cases #3, #5, #6, and #7) using the TruSight RNA Pan-Cancer Panel. Sequencing could not be performed for one case (case #5) due to insufficient RNA yield. But none of the sequenced cases exhibited fusions in RTK genes, including ALK, ROS1, MET, and NTRK1/2/3. Both the TruSight RNA Pan-Cancer Panel and the confirmation sequencing study (details provided in the Methods section) identified a TMEM106B::BRAF fusion in one case (case #6). This fusion involved the 10th exon of the BRAF gene and the 3rd exon of the TMEM106B gene.

Additionally, sequencing data were also analyzed using SNV-InDel calling pipelines, but no BRAF SNVs or InDels were detected in the 3 real-time PCR-negative cases in either of the NGS studies. Histomorphological and molecular characteristics of all tumors are displayed in Table 3.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: DIG/DIA is an exceedingly rare tumor typically observed in early pediatric patients. This WHO grade 1 tumor is almost exclusively seen in the first 2 years of life but may rarely present later. [19][20][21] Though multifocal tumor, suprasellar and spinal masses have been reported, DIG/DIA almost always presents as a single large supratentorial mass having cystic and solid components. [22][23][24][25] To provide a clearer overview of the clinicopathological spectrum of this rare entity, we conducted a comprehensive review of the literature and systematically summarized all DIG/DIA cases reported in between 2015 and 2025 with their essential characteristics (Table 4).

Diagnosing these tumors can be quite challenging, particularly considering the similarities they share with "infant-type hemispheric glioma (IHG), " a tumor type introduced in 2021. 2 Despite the clinical similarities in age of onset and location, DIG/DIA and IHG may be distinguished by a combination of histological architecture and immunohistochemical profile. 26 DIG/DIA exhibits a distinctive biphasic architecture characterized by desmoplastic, spindle-cell-rich areas intermingled with primitive-looking regions-a hallmark feature of this tumor type. Mitotic activity is low in desmoplastic areas, and necrosis, microvascular proliferation is absent. In contrast, IHGs are usually highly cellular diffuse glial tumors sometimes resembling adult type high grade diffuse glioma. These tumors frequently show brisk mitotic activity, (palisading) necrosis, and microvascular proliferation. 13 Desmoplasia is not a feature of IHG, although in our experience, can rarely be observed. Recognition of these features is essential but may not be adequate for the diagnosis. Molecular findings are also very helpful and showing MAPK alterations (specifically BRAF mutations) would favor a DIG/DIA diagnosis in the setting of a low-grade tumor with classical morphological features described above; and showing a RTK gene fusion would strongly favor a diagnosis of IHG in the setting of a high-grade diffuse glial tumor morphology. However, it is important to note that multiple groups have reported that infantile glial tumors with RTK fusions may cluster within the DIG/DIA methylation class using the Heidelberg CNS Tumor Classifier. Likewise, tumors without detectable

div.head: Kulac et al.: Morphomolecular and clinical evaluation of DIG/DIAs
div.p: genetic alterations can also classify as DIG/DIA or IHG on methylation profiling, although detailed histological descriptions of such reported cases are often lacking. These findings highlight the diagnostic difficulty in distinguishing DIG/DIA from infant-type hemispheric glioma even when genomic and transcriptomic data are available, as not all (methylation-based classified) infant-type hemispheric gliomas harbor RTK fusions and not all (methylation-based classified) DIG/DIAs exhibit MAPK pathway alterations. [26][27][28][29] Nevertheless, identification of driver molecular alterations may open the door to targeted therapies; anti-RAF or anti-MEK treatment for DIG/ DIA, anti-RTK treatment for IHG. 30,31 All DIG/DIAs in our series had prominent desmoplastic areas which can be highlighted by reticulin stain, and this feature is one of the most helpful features for the evaluating pathologist. Embryonal-looking primitive areas on the other hand was not that pronounced in many cases, may even be a small focus even in a very large tumor. Areas of primitive cells, on the other hand, may show high mitosis as well as a propensity to call the tumor high grade, if undersampled, by an unexperienced pathologist. Although primitive areas in some tumors in our series exhibited an exceedingly high mitotic count, we did not observe aggressive clinical course (Table 2). Although the small sample size precludes meaningful statistical analysis, it is noteworthy that none of our patients have died from the disease. Recurrences were observed in some cases, yet all patients remain in good clinical condition. Similar favorable outcomes for DIG/DIA have been reported in the literature, mostly in case reports or small series with relatively short follow-up periods. In contrast, our series provides longer-term data, with a median follow-up of 68 months. 26,32,33 Histologically, we also found that the primitive areas and astrocytic components were not sharply demarcated; rather, transitions between the two patterns were gradual, and intermediate morphological forms were frequently encountered. Moreover, these tumors are largely composed of GFAP-positive, glial-appearing areas that exhibit a morphological appearance between embryonal and glial phenotypes. Another important feature deserving attention is the involvement of the Virchow-Robin spaces, presenting as a perivascular growth pattern, which was also mentioned in the results section (see Table 3).

The observation of a relatively infiltrative growth pattern in some of the cases contradicts the traditional classification of DIG/DIA as a circumscribed tumor. Not all low-grade circumscribed astrocytic gliomas have well-defined borders, as is often observed in pilocytic astrocytomas. 34 This highlights the increasing need to distinguish DIG/DIA from other infantile gliomas, particularly infant-type hemispheric gliomas, which are inherently diffuse. Additionally, microscopic leptomeningeal dissemination was observed in 3 cases-a known phenomenon in these tumors-but it does not appear to impact prognosis. Moreover, there is an unusual example of a DIG/ DIA reported in the literature with extensive extensive leptomeningeal dissemination mimicking diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumor. 21 Given these findings, recognizing the broad morphological spectrum of DIG/DIA is essential for ensuring accurate diagnosis and appropriate clinical management.

Anaplastic features such as necrosis or microvascular proliferation are reported only rarely in DIG/DIA. Megias et al 35 documented a desmoplastic infantile astrocytoma with a BRAF p.V600E mutation and homozygous PTEN deletion that exhibited anaplastic histology. They proposed that PTEN loss might drive more aggressive behavior, but this could not be confirmed because the patient died just days after surgery. Another case report described malignant transformation 8 years after initial diagnosis; that tumor was BRAF wild-type and potential fusion events were not explored. 36 All but one case in our series were diagnosed during infancy. Case #4 was diagnosed at the age of 3. It exhibited classical DIG/DIA morphology, with both desmoplastic and primitive components, and harbored BRAF p. V600E mutation. Consistent with prior reports, DIG/DIA cases diagnosed outside infancy is rare but do not appear to show significant differences compared to those diagnosed during infancy; but most of those cases reported lacked morphological definitions and molecular evidence for DIG/DIA diagnosis. 21,23,[37][38][39][40][41][42][43] The literature occasionally reports DIG/DIA in association with other conditions-most commonly focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) and, more rarely, multiple sclerosis (MS) or Down syndrome. 38,39,44,45 In line with these observations, we also identified overlapping findings in our series: one case demonstrated cortical lamination disorganization consistent with FCD, while another exhibited an associated vascular pathology.

We aimed to determine whether antibodies against ALK, ROS1, and pan-TRK showed any positivity in our cases. Although no pathogenic fusions were detected, we observed some immunoreactivity with these antibodies. Notably, focal ALK positivity and diffuse yet weak pan-TRK positivity in isolated cases raise concerns about potential diagnostic pitfalls, as these findings could mimic RTK-driven gliomas. In parallel with previous studies, pan-TRK antibody was found to be unreliable for screening NTRK fusions in CNS tumors because of high positivity rates caused by physiological expression. 46,47 This underscores the critical need for molecular confirmation to prevent misdiagnosis.

Although tumors of this type are expected to harbor alterations in MAPK pathway genes, particularly in BRAF, 29 no pathogenic alterations were identified in 3 out of 8 cases. Notably, these 3 cases exhibited classical DIG/DIA morphology with pronounced desmoplasia and primitive areas, and 48,50 While BRAF mutation testing by real-time PCR is a common diagnostic approach for these tumors, our findings underscore the need for awareness of alternative BRAF alterations, such as fusions. RNA-based sequencing panels serve as powerful tools for detecting these fusion events. Consistent with our findings, other research groups have also reported BRAF or RAF1 alterations in low-grade pediatric gliomas, 11,12,48 further highlighting the clinical and biological significance of these molecular events. These findings support the expansion of molecular testing in cases considered to be DIG/DIA but lacking the BRAF p. V600E mutation.

This study has certain limitations. Morphologically, the cases demonstrated highly similar features, and, as expected, most harbored BRAF alterations. Two cases, however, were histologically indistinguishable from the others but did not show any detectable MAPK pathway alterations. As comprehensive DNA-based analyses were not performed, we cannot fully exclude the presence of undetected MAPK pathway changes. Nevertheless, RTK fusions were confidently excluded and therefore these 2 cases with classical morphology were considered "likely DIG/DIA. " In addition, another case in our series was negative for the BRAF p. V600 mutation, but due to insufficient RNA quality, NGS analysis could not be performed; this case should also be regarded as "likely DIG/DIA. " Although methylation profiling could have provided further insights, it was not performed due to financial constraints.

Although numerous case reports and small series have been published in the literature (most of them has already been discussed in this paper), each of them has notable limitations. Some provide detailed clinical data but lack molecular analyses, while others present molecular findings without adequate histopathological characterization. As a result, none offers a truly comprehensive perspective. In this context, our study stands out by integrating clinical, histopathological, and molecular features, representing one of the most comprehensive case series reported to date. While this study provides valuable insights into the morphological and molecular spectrum of DIG/DIA, specifically introducing a new BRAF fusion described in DIG/DIAs for the first time in the literature, its retrospective design and limited sample size pose some limitations. In the future, our aim will be conducting larger, longitudinal, preferably multicenter studies to better understand the clinical behavior and prognostic factors associated with this rare tumor type.
